So the idea of contrastive learning
is you're going to get pairs that are similar
and pairs that are dissimilar, and you
want to pull the similar pairs together and push
the dissimilar pairs apart.
And the way that you usually do this
in the context of self-supervised learning
is you're going to start with your input images.
And again, these are unlabeled images.
You don't have labels for them.
And now for each input image, you're
going to apply two random transformations.

So basically for each one of your input images,
you're going to apply two or possibly more than two,

Now you're going to feed all of those randomly perturbed

Then you want to apply this notion of contrastive.

we want to push them apart.
So you basically run all of these things through

4n squared matrix of all of your scaler similarities between

And to really appreciate what's going on probabilistically,

When you talk about a probability distribution or more
generally, a density function p of x,
p of x is basically a function that assigns a nonzero
number to every possible input x with the very important
normalization constraint, that if you integrate over
the entire space of all possible x's, it integrates to 1.
And this normalization constraint
really gives rise to the power of probabilistic models
in some sense because the normalization constraint
means that all of your x's need to compete for probability mass.
There's a fixed unit amount of probability mass,
and choosing a probability distribution or density function
basically amounts to apportioning out
that fixed amount of probability mass
and smearing it across all possible values of x
that could exist.
And all of those x's are in competition
because there's only a fixed unit
amount of mass to go around.
So if you want to push up the probability of one x,
necessarily, the probabilities or densities
of other x's have to go down.
And so then in these different formulations

competing for probability mass.
And that means that even though the symbols that we write

among what is competing for probability mass
induces very different structure that the model is
trying to learn or uncover.
So in the case of a discriminative model,

of y conditioned on x, which means that for every x,
our model is predicting a probability distribution

And we have a separate probability distribution

Because every image is inducing its own distribution

The only things that are competing for mass
